# How to read this book {.unnumbered}

You don't have to read it front to back. Here are three routes, depending on where you're starting.

![Three routes through the book's seven parts.](/figures/front/paths.pdf){#fig-paths}

**If you're new to machine learning**, read it in order. Part I builds the foundation everything else rests on: probabilities, and how to turn them into actions you can defend. Parts II and III explain neural networks, embeddings, attention, LLMs and agents without assuming you've met any of them before.

**If you already build with LLMs**, read Part I anyway, and don't skip Chapter 4 on calibration or Chapter 5 on costs. Then jump to Part IV. The rest of the book leans on those two chapters more than on anything else.

**If you lead a team or a product**, read Part I, then Chapters 15 to 21, then Chapters 25 and 29. You'll skip the code-heavy chapters and still be able to ask your team the right questions: what does a mistake cost, where's the line, how do we know the probabilities are honest, and who reads the flags?

## The boxes

![The boxes you'll meet in every chapter.](/figures/front/boxes.pdf){#fig-boxes}

Each chapter opens with a short list of what you'll be able to do by the end, and closes with a short recap, exercises and a hook to the next chapter. In between, a few kinds of box recur (@fig-boxes). The *Try it* boxes contain code you can run; the *Set the threshold* boxes ask you to make a small decision with real costs; the *Where this breaks* boxes are the honest limits of what the chapter just showed. Read those last ones. They're the difference between knowing a technique and knowing when to trust it.

## Running the code

Every listing in the book runs, and a test in the book's repository checks that it still does. The labs are Jupyter notebooks. Chapter 1's lab is `labs/ch01.ipynb`, Chapter 2's is `labs/ch02.ipynb`, and so on; each one opens in Google Colab and installs everything it needs.

To run things on your own machine:

```bash
pip install typesafe-sdk==0.7.2
pip install git+https://github.com/Mukkandi-Sridhar/JEVBook
```

The second line installs `jevkit`, the book's toolkit. Among other things, it includes the mock that answers the official SDK's calls without a network connection or an API key. If you have a real TypeSafe API key, set `JEVKIT_LIVE=1` and `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`, and the labs call the real service instead; Chapter 23 explains how.

## The companion widgets

Four small browser tools let you move the book's numbers yourself: a threshold simulator (Chapter 21), a calibration playground (Chapters 4 and 18), a bake-off explorer (Chapter 20) and a decision cost calculator (Chapters 16, 19 and 23). They're in the `site/` folder of the repository and on the book's website, and they run entirely in your browser.

## A word on the numbers

Kestrel Logistics is fictional, and so are its alerts, which come from a generator with a known truth behind every one. That's what makes it possible to measure things exactly, like how many real threats a policy misses. It also means every number is an illustration of a method, not a fact about the world. When a figure is labelled *synthetic*, believe the shape and test the numbers on your own data.
